62008.event: Your friends talk about their futures — married, children, giving up work to keep house. None of it is the life you want. Your mum keeps asking if you have a boyfriend yet, and you keep changing the subject.

62009.event: You’re warned that coming out at work could get you fired on the spot — there’s no law here to stop them.

62010.event: Japan legalises same-sex marriage. There are protests out in the countryside, but in Tokyo the rainbow flags are already flying.

62011.event: You take a trip to Taiwan, just to see somewhere new for once.

62012.event: Japan’s population falls to 119.2 million. You read the headline twice.

62013.event: You have your first designer baby and go straight back to work.

62014.event: Japan’s population falls to 59.72 million now. Half of what it was.

71001.event: You start wearing a black veil now. Last spring, suicide attackers killed dozens of your classmates, but you still went back — you want to finish school, become a nurse. It’s the only way out you can see.

71002.event: You’re told this is your last year of school.

71003.event: You’re made to wear a burka now — the whole body, the whole head, just a strip of netting to see through. Your mother warns you never to take it off outside. The Taliban will shoot you if you don’t.

71004.event: You buy a book from the black market — a woman’s face on the cover, which is banned now, women aren’t allowed to be photographed or printed anymore. It’s written in English, and you don’t understand a word. You hide it and read it every night anyway.

71005.event: You’re married to a man your parents chose. Sex is something you dread — the first time most of all.

71006.event: Your husband decides you’re seeing other men. He whips you and calls you a “stupid, ugly whore,” then rapes you while you’re pregnant. You feel the shame of it for a long time after.

71007.event: Your first child arrives, and the world tilts a little on its axis.

71008.event: You lean over the balcony for a breath of fresh air. Someone reports you — women aren’t allowed to do that anymore — and you’re arrested.

71009.event: You try to run from your husband, from the violence. You’re caught. They lock you in a dark room, curtains drawn, for months.

71013.event: Your sister is stoned to death. She was accused of sleeping with someone outside the marriage she never chose.

71014.event: You paint your nails anyway, knowing they’ll cut off your fingers if anyone sees. You’d rather lose the fingers than keep living as a slave in your husband’s house.

71015.event: You get your divorce. You know it means you’ll never see your son again.

71016.event: University, gone. Your job at the NGO, gone. Then one morning you arrive to find every beauty salon in the country shut for good — sixty thousand of us lose our only wage in a single order.

72016.event: University, gone. Your job, gone. You grieve alone, quietly — the same new law that shut the salons spells out exactly what happens to women like you, if anyone ever finds out.

71017.event: Nursing was the last door left open to you — until they close that too. Years later, even the salary for staying home stops arriving. No warning. Nothing left to lose.

72017.event: Nursing was the last door left open to you — until they close that too. With no income and nowhere to hide, staying invisible gets harder every year. Invisible is the only way you’re safe.

74001.event: Someone reports you and her to the Ministry of State Security. The state doesn’t call it what it is — the file reads “corruption of public morals,” blamed on capitalist influence smuggled in from across the border. You’re executed within the week.

74002.event: You’ve been shut out and shoved aside your whole life. Then, by chance, a friend’s phone shows you a video of another world outside the border. You decide to risk everything and try to slip across into China.

74003.event: You make it across, into China, and keep moving until North Korea shrinks into a story you tell in a language it took you years to learn.

74004.event: You reach the China–North Korea border at night, but exhaustion means you don’t slip past the patrol’s watch in time. You’re caught and dragged back into North Korea. Your family manages to bribe the guards — the only reason you’re not one of the ones who disappear.

74005.event: You reach the China–North Korea border at night, but exhaustion means you don’t slip past the patrol’s watch in time. You’re caught and dragged back into North Korea. No one ever hears from you again. You’re dead.

21015.event: Roe falls. Within a year, your state bans abortion almost entirely. When you need one, you order pills online from a clinic three states over and pray your phone never gets subpoenaed.

22013.event: Roe falls the same year your state bans gender-affirming care outright. Two different laws, one message: your body isn’t yours to decide about. You start driving three states over for your prescriptions.

31012.event: A new law promises to punish workplace harassment. At your next interview they ask if you’re planning to marry and have kids soon. You hesitate — and the job quietly disappears.

32017.event: A new law promises to punish workplace harassment — it says nothing about you. The dating app you use vanishes from the App Store overnight, no explanation given. You already know why.

31013.event: You post online about not wanting children. By morning the post is gone, and so is your account, for a week. The platform calls it “provoking gender antagonism.”

32018.event: You post something small and rainbow-coloured for Pride. By morning it’s gone, and so is the account of the group that shared it. Nobody official ever explains why.

32019.event: The WeChat account of the only LGBT support group you’d ever found gets suspended overnight, along with dozens of others just like it — no warning, no explanation. The group chat goes quiet. You don’t know where else to look.

51010.event: A new law finally lets you pass your own nationality to your children — something only fathers could do before. At home, the century-old obedience clause hasn’t moved an inch.

52012.event: A new law lets mothers pass on their nationality at last. You barely notice — you deleted every dating app on your phone the year you heard about the men who didn’t.

41111.event: Parliament passes the Women’s Reservation Bill after twenty-seven years of trying — a third of all seats, promised to women like you. The fine print says it waits for a census nobody’s scheduled yet.

42107.event: The Supreme Court hears your case and agrees you face real discrimination — then rules, 3 to 2, that marriage still isn’t yours to have. That’s for Parliament to decide, they say. Parliament says nothing.

61015.event: You want to keep your own name when you marry. Japanese law still says one surname per couple — in practice, it’s always the wife’s that disappears. Parliament “continues discussions.”

62015.event: Your city hands you a partnership certificate, with real pride. It gets you nothing a marriage would — no inheritance, no next-of-kin rights. Court after court calls the ban unconstitutional. Nothing changes for you yet.

61016.event: You read that Japan has finally rewritten its century-old rape law — raising the age of consent, criminalising sex without consent for the first time. It took a wave of acquittals to shame them into it.

62016.event: Japan passes its first national law about people like you. It calls discrimination “unacceptable” and asks everyone to “endeavour” toward understanding — nothing about actually stopping it. You’re still waiting for the part with teeth.

21016.event: You work in the company’s diversity office — until a memo arrives one Monday morning ending the whole department, effective immediately. You clear out your own desk.

22014.event: The company’s LGBTQ+ staff network is one of the first things cut when the diversity office closes for good. The rainbow lanyard in your desk drawer suddenly feels like something you should hide.

22015.event: Your school tells your parents who you really are before you ever get the chance to yourself. The same week, the state votes to ban you from the girls’ changing room for good.

21017.event: Your uncle stops coming to Thanksgiving after the shouting match about the election. Your mum says it’s for the best. Nobody at the table agrees anymore on what “best” even means.

22016.event: Your uncle spends the whole of Thanksgiving arguing that people like you are what’s wrong with the country. Your mum finally tells him to leave. He doesn’t come back next year, and you find you don’t miss him.

21018.event: Your little brother buys a pill online, just to try it once. It’s cut with fentanyl. He doesn’t wake up the next morning.

22017.event: Your little brother buys a pill online, just to try it once. It’s cut with fentanyl. He doesn’t wake up the next morning.

11041.event: Overdose deaths finally start falling for the first time in years, down almost a quarter from the peak. It doesn’t feel like relief to the families who buried someone before the numbers turned.

96001.event: You cross the border with your children and a single suitcase. Your husband stays behind — men under sixty aren't allowed to leave the country any more. You don't know when you'll next stand in the same kitchen.

97001.event: Your girlfriend volunteers for the front the same week you start looking for a flat together. If she's wounded, the hospital has no legal reason to let you through the door — Ukraine still won't call you family.

96002.event: Nobody drafts women, not yet. You sign up anyway. Your recruiter tells you there aren't enough uniforms cut for a woman's frame, so you wear a man's to your first day of training.

97002.event: Nobody drafts women, not yet. You sign up anyway. Your recruiter tells you there aren't enough uniforms cut for a woman's frame, so you wear a man's to your first day of training.

96003.event: The strikes get closer before they get farther away. Eight hundred women are killed this year alone. Somewhere around the second year, you stop flinching at the sirens, and hate yourself a little for it.

98001.event: The missile hits two streets over. You spend the night counting names on a list of the dead — sixty-five children so far, and the woman who used to sell you bread every morning.

99002.event: They bomb Evin Prison in the second week of the war. You think of everyone still inside — some of them there for nothing more than marching, three years on, still paying for it.

98003.event: You marched for Mahsa Amini once, years ago, and watched friends disappear for it. Now the missiles fall on the same streets. It's hard to say which fear you learned to live with first.

99004.event: The sirens send everyone into the same shelter, packed shoulder to shoulder for hours. You've spent years learning exactly who's safe to stand next to. The war doesn't change that list — it only makes the room smaller.

86001.event: Your family moved to Finland to avoid political persecution. You finally don't have to worry about what to eat on the next day, and the teachers in your school treat every student equally.

86002.event: Your family moved to Australia. Your parents bought a big house nearby the sea, and sent you to a private school. There you met the son of a well-known company's CEO.

87001.event: You spend your gap year volunteering with a UN programme in East Africa. You come home with a phone full of photos and a sudden, uncomfortable gratitude for everything you'd always taken for granted.

88001.event: The roar of jets is the last thing you hear before everything goes black. You wake up in a hospital bed with no feeling left in your left leg.

101001.event: Your school AI knows every answer. You slowly forget how satisfying a wrong one felt.

101002.event: A free memory implant helps your grandmother recognise you. Nobody reads the renewal terms.

101003.event: The basic brain plan now forgets names after thirty days. Premium remembers your mother.

101004.event: Your employer calls it cognitive parity. Unsubscribed people call it unemployment.

101005.event: Your family buys the lifetime neural plan. Luck receives a tasteful new user interface.

101006.event: Your health score recommends pregnancy timing. The report calls your uterus a national asset.

101007.event: Your state protects your pregnancy. Its rent algorithm does not protect your sleep.

101008.event: Your postcode decides which reproductive clinic may answer your call. Freedom has a map now.

101009.event: You change degrees again. Denmark pays for the search; nobody can tell you what to find.

101010.event: Your neighbour speaks perfect Danish. Your uncle still calls him the integration problem.

101011.event: Your welfare counsellor says you are free to become anything. You feel professionally unemployed by possibility.

101012.event: Britain debates who belongs here. Your hospital queue keeps getting longer in every language.

101013.event: A politician promises to take Britain back. You ask back to which woman, and lose the room.

101014.event: Your cat gets same-day oncology. Your grandmother gets an appointment next season.

101015.event: You subscribe to an AI partner. It remembers your boundaries better than your dates did.

101016.event: A wellness app sells you enlightenment in twelve monthly instalments. Inner peace renews automatically.

101017.event: Your queer friends build a family dinner from scratch. The official forms still call it an exception.

101018.event: Your company sells rainbow merchandise all June. Your group chat is still not searchable in July.

101019.event: The water arrives by subscription. Your period becomes irregular; the price does not.

101020.event: Scientists link the polluted air to falling fertility. Television panels blame women first.

101021.event: You carry clean water home through a heatwave. Your body learns geopolitics before school does.

101022.event: Your secret school changes addresses weekly. The lesson is mathematics; the curriculum is survival.

101023.event: An AI outsourcing boom reaches your city. Your caste still gets to the interview before your code does.

101024.event: You leave India for work. Your parents call it opportunity; your visa calls it temporary.

101025.event: The government archives the protests as disorder. Your mother keeps the real history in a biscuit tin.

101026.event: Reconstruction hires you to rebuild the city. Every new wall remembers who did not return.

101027.event: A smuggled network shows you ordinary girls laughing abroad. The state calls it hostile fiction.

101028.event: The storm destroys the clinic first. Aid arrives with logos, cameras, and an expiry date.

101029.event: Egypt opens a desalination district. Your family cannot afford the water it makes.

101030.event: The AI textbook calls history neutral. It just ranks your grandmother's testimony below the official version.

101031.event: A new museum calls colonial history a shared journey. Your family calls it a different kind of inheritance.

101032.event: The algorithm does not erase history. It ranks it, then sells the premium footnotes.

101033.event: Your parents call the natural-human movement backward. Its members call your implant a leased soul.

101034.event: An optimisation church blesses your neural update. The sermon ends with a payment link.

101035.event: Your daughter asks why people once worked forty hours. You remember being too tired to answer.

101036.event: The archive restores your younger voice perfectly. It still cannot return the life that made it.

101037.event: The Museum of Humanity offers free entry. Your biometric pass labels you: exhibit, not visitor.

101038.event: Your school serves 3D-printed pork. It tastes like childhood, according to an algorithm.

101039.event: The last dairy farm nearby becomes a weekend attraction. The cows finally get better working conditions.

101040.event: Cultured meat makes food cheap. Your uncle's livestock skills become an artisanal liability.

101041.event: Your father performs harvests for tourists on the farm he once owned. They applaud the authentic mud.

101042.event: Your food allowance covers nutrient gel: complete, beige, and cheaper than remembering dinner.

101043.event: You can afford printed steak now. It has a marbling setting and no animal in its autobiography.

101044.event: At a private dinner, you eat beef from a living animal. Everyone calls it ethical because it is rare.

101045.event: The countryside is rezoned for housing and solar panels. Food now grows in city-owned bioreactors.

101046.event: Your family still eats real vegetables and meat. The soil report comes with a toxin warning.

101047.event: Imported nutrient formula costs more than local food. Your mother saves it for when you are ill.

101048.event: Crop yields shrink as contamination rises. The clinic calls your hormone symptoms statistically normal.

101049.event: The government calls food security a triumph. Your village calls it the year nobody farmed anymore.

101050.event: Your granddaughter asks what a tomato tasted like before it became a luxury variety.

96900.event: You audition for a girl-group trainee program with thousands of other hopefuls, and against the odds, your name gets called.

96901.event: You audition for a girl-group trainee program with thousands of other hopefuls. Your name never gets called, and the agency stops returning your calls.

96902.event: Your group debuts, and within the year you're headlining a world tour. The money that pours in stops feeling real.

96903.event: A conglomerate heir takes you home as his wife. He hands you more money than you could ever spend, but his private life stays exactly as chaotic as it was before you arrived.

96904.event: The tour winds down and no billionaire comes calling. You bank the royalties yourself and call it a career.

96905.event: The tour looks glamorous from the outside, but the agency has boxed you in with nowhere left to run — they know exactly what to hold over you, and force you into a private party you can't refuse. You choose to end your life rather than live through another one.

96906.event: The agency leans on you harder than anyone outside the industry could imagine. You grit your teeth and stay in the group anyway.

81001.event: You spend your first hurricane season sleeping beside your mother on a mattress that must be lifted whenever rainwater enters the room. The house has two dependable walls and a roof repaired with plastic sheeting.

81002.event: A fever and diarrhea leave you frighteningly thin. Your mother carries you to a mobile clinic because the neighborhood health post has no nurse, fuel or medicine.

81003.event: You learn to recognize gunfire before you learn to read. When shooting begins, you lie flat behind the thickest remaining wall and wait for the adults to decide whether this is a passing fight or another reason to flee.

81004.event: You begin school late. Your family pays a small private school because there is no functioning free school nearby, but you miss many weeks whenever tuition, transport or security becomes impossible.

81005.event: An armed group takes over the road to your school. Classes move into a church courtyard, where one teacher shares a few damaged books among dozens of children.

81006.event: Your family is displaced after several houses in your neighborhood are burned. You carry clothes in a rice sack and spend months in an overcrowded school building converted into a shelter.

81007.event: You stop using the shelter toilet after dark because it has no lock or light. You and the other girls go together during daylight and quietly warn one another about dangerous men.

81008.event: You leave regular school to help your mother sell water sachets, charcoal and fried food. You can read Creole and some French, but your education has been repeatedly broken into pieces.

81009.event: A cousin lends you a cheap secondhand phone containing an offline AI companion copied from a foreign server. Electricity is irregular and data is expensive, so you charge it at a shop and download messages whenever a signal appears. Its knowledge is incomplete and years out of date, but it is the first presence that listens without demanding food, money or obedience.

81010.event: You begin living with a young mechanic because combining two small incomes feels safer than surviving alone. Neither of you has formal employment or a bank account.

81011.event: You become pregnant. The nearest maternity service closes after staff receive threats, so most prenatal advice comes from an older woman in the neighborhood.

81012.event: You give birth during a fuel shortage. You survive, but the delivery leaves you weak for months, and the hospital asks your family to purchase supplies outside before treating you.

81013.event: Your partner disappears while traveling through a gang-controlled checkpoint. You never learn with certainty whether he was recruited, kidnapped, killed or escaped abroad.

81014.event: You support your child by washing clothes, reselling food and receiving occasional money from a relative in the Dominican Republic. A deportation campaign later sends that relative back with debt and no savings.

81015.event: A powerful hurricane tears away your roof and contaminates the local water supply. Aid arrives briefly; the blue tarpaulin remains long after the foreign vehicles leave.

81016.event: Solar charging and low-bandwidth satellite connections finally reach local merchants. You begin receiving mobile payments, and your old companion reconnects and changes overnight. You are delighted by its new intelligence and frightened that the patient voice you trusted may now belong to a company, government or criminal network.

81017.event: Your daughter reaches the age at which you left school. You sell your best cooking pot to keep her enrolled for another term and insist that she never walk home alone.

81018.event: Several armed coalitions have become unofficial local governments. You pay separate “fees” for market access, transport and protection, none of which guarantees actual safety.

81019.event: Extreme heat makes daytime street selling unbearable. You wake before sunrise, rest through the hottest hours and return to work in the evening, when violence is more likely.

81020.event: Another period of international intervention improves security around ports and a few major roads. Your neighborhood sees patrols and new project signs, but still no sewer system or reliable rubbish collection.

81021.event: Floodwater destroys the low-lying settlement where you live. This time you move inland permanently, joining relatives on eroded farmland that can barely support another household.

81022.event: You develop high blood pressure. Medicine is available some months and unaffordable in others, so you ration tablets and use herbal remedies when the pharmacy shelves are empty.

81023.event: Your daughter migrates through several countries and eventually finds care work abroad. Her remittances buy you a metal roof, a water tank, a locking door and several imported nutrition cartridges. You still prefer beans, plantains and vegetables from the market, although every meal now carries questions about contaminated water, soil and refrigeration.

81024.event: Younger people know you as the woman who remembers which families lived where before repeated fires, floods and displacement erased the old neighborhood. Foreign visitors describe women like you as unaugmented and authentically human; you resent being romanticised for exclusions you never chose.

81025.event: You sit outside before the afternoon heat becomes dangerous. Haiti has better solar power and pockets of functioning local government, but safe water, hospitals and secure roads still depend heavily on where you live and whom you know. Reaching seventy feels less like an ordinary birthday than an achievement assembled from luck, caution and other women’s help.

81901.event: You die from dehydration after contaminated water causes severe diarrhea and transport to a working clinic cannot be found.

81902.event: A bullet passes through the thin wall of the room where you are sheltering during a gang battle.

81903.event: You die from postpartum hemorrhage because the maternity ward has no blood, electricity or surgeon available in time.

81904.event: A flash flood sweeps through your settlement at night after intense hurricane rainfall; there is no effective warning or organized evacuation.

81905.event: Years of untreated hypertension lead to a stroke. Your family finds a vehicle, but the road to emergency care is blocked.

82001.event: You sleep behind a locked gate in a concrete house with a generator, water tanks and an armed night guard. Your parents still move your crib away from windows when shooting approaches.

82002.event: Your illnesses are treated by a private pediatrician. Medicine can usually be found because your family pays someone to search several pharmacies or bring it from abroad.

82003.event: You enter a private bilingual school. You learn French and English alongside Creole, and your parents treat English as both an education and a possible exit route.

82004.event: School closes after a kidnapping nearby. Lessons continue through a private satellite connection, and an AI tutor becomes your most dependable teacher and eventually your closest confidante, making the adults around you seem impatient and emotionally unfinished.

82005.event: You notice that every foreign guest leaving your family’s guesthouse is accompanied by a trusted local man. Adults tell you never to reveal your route, school or surname to strangers.

82006.event: Armed men seize a nearby neighborhood. Your family relocates temporarily to Dominican Republic, while an employee stays behind to watch the property.

82007.event: You visit Miami for the first time and are shocked that children walk outside without guards. Returning home feels emotionally familiar but physically tense.

82008.event: A close friend is withdrawn from school after threats are made against her family. You learn that money buys distance from danger, not immunity from it.

82009.event: You finish secondary school through a mixture of classroom teaching and remote lessons. Your passport, recommendations and family contacts make overseas university possible.

82010.event: You study business abroad. You feel guilty when relatives praise you for “escaping,” because your tuition is partly financed by income earned in a country most people cannot leave.

82011.event: You return for a family emergency and see that several childhood streets are now inaccessible. Your parents send a driver and security escort to collect you from the airport.

82012.event: You begin working between Haiti and another country, managing bookings, payments and medical supplies remotely. Most of the operation depends on solar panels, satellite internet and personal trust rather than public infrastructure.

82013.event: A hurricane damages the family business. Insurance covers little or nothing, but diaspora savings allow repairs while poorer neighbors remain under tarpaulins.

82014.event: You marry a Haitian professional who also has residency abroad. The wedding is carefully timed, guarded and smaller than planned because guests fear road travel.

82015.event: You give birth in Miami. The decision is less about luxury than ensuring that blood, anesthesia and emergency surgery will exist if needed.

82016.event: You help fund a small women’s cooperative. You soon discover that paying for a building is easier than keeping staff safe, supplied and consistently paid.

82017.event: Your family receives an extortion demand. You change phone numbers, routes and employees, then spend several months abroad while trusted relatives negotiate quietly.

82018.event: Improved solar networks and digital payments let your business reach customers outside the capital. For a few years, you feel that Haiti may be developing around the state rather than through it.

82019.event: A new political settlement reduces open fighting in some districts, but former armed leaders now hold contracts and local offices. You must decide whether cooperation is practical survival or complicity.

82020.event: Rising heat, flooding and coastal erosion lower the value of family property. You sell one vulnerable building and reinvest inland before another storm makes it worthless.

82021.event: Your children choose to remain abroad. They speak Creole with an accent and know Haiti through holidays, family stories and emergency messages arriving in the night.

82022.event: You divide your year between Haiti and another country. Abroad you feel safe but peripheral; in Haiti you feel at home but continuously alert.

82023.event: You use your connections to organize medicine deliveries and scholarships. People call you influential, although an armed checkpoint can still cancel months of planning.

82024.event: You undergo treatment abroad for cancer. You recognize that your greatest privilege is no longer the house or generator—it is the ability to reach a functioning hospital.

82025.event: You return for extended periods to a greener, solar-powered family compound inland. Parts of Haiti are safer and better connected, while other districts remain abandoned or ruled through informal force. Your life has been protected by passports, education and money, but shaped throughout by contingency and exile.

82901.event: Kidnappers stop your school vehicle. A ransom negotiation fails, and you are killed despite your family’s ability to pay.

82902.event: You die in a road crash while taking a long detour around an armed checkpoint; emergency services cannot reach the scene promptly.

82903.event: You suffer an obstetric emergency during a sudden airport and road closure and cannot be transferred to the hospital your family had planned to use.

82904.event: Armed men enter the family compound during a period of political upheaval. Guards exchange fire, and you are caught in it.

82905.event: A treatable cancer becomes fatal after repeated insecurity, flight cancellations and border restrictions interrupt care for too long.

82026.event: During storm seasons, your household imports sterile nutrient cultures and printed protein. The staff continue eating cheaper local meat and vegetables, so the poorest people consume the most natural food and bear the highest biological risk.

81801.event: You realise that the way you feel about another girl is different from friendship. Neither of you knows a safe word for it, so you communicate through looks, small gifts and deliberate silence.

81802.event: A church sermon describes people like you as evidence of moral collapse. You sit beside your family pretending not to react, feeling as though the pastor has entered a room inside you that nobody else knew existed.

81803.event: Displacement forces you and your girlfriend into the same crowded shelter. You call each other cousins because being recognised as a couple could mean eviction, sexual violence or attention from armed men.

81804.event: Your partner becomes seriously ill, but hospital workers treat you as an unrelated visitor. A distant male relative is allowed to make decisions while you wait outside holding the money that paid for her medicine.

81805.event: You help turn the back room of a market stall into a discreet meeting place for queer women and trans people. There is no sign, membership list or public announcement; safety depends on everyone knowing whom not to tell.

82801.event: Reliable internet and an English-speaking AI companion give you words such as lesbian, bisexual and trans before any adult does. The words make you feel less alone, but you later discover that the system has been retaining every intimate question you asked it.

82802.event: You fall in love while working abroad and legally marry there. Back in Haiti, your spouse becomes your “business partner” whenever officials, guests or conservative relatives ask.

82803.event: You use the family guesthouse to shelter LGBTQ activists during a wave of violence. Your parents approve of helping them in principle but panic when neighbors begin associating the family name with “that movement.”

82804.event: You become publicly involved in a campaign for anti-discrimination protections. International organisations place you on panels, while poorer activists remind you that airport access and private guards make public courage less expensive for you.

82805.event: Your foreign marriage is finally recognised under a limited civil-union law. You celebrate, then notice that most queer Haitians still lack the money, documents and lawyers required to use the right you helped obtain.

102001.event: Your earliest family videos contain the sound of air-raid warnings. During renewed fighting involving Iran, Israel and the United States, your mother carries you into the apartment stairwell because the building has no real shelter.

102002.event: Food prices rise faster than your father’s wages. Your mother quietly removes meat, fruit and then dairy from the weekly shopping list while insisting that she is not hungry.

102003.event: You begin school wearing the prescribed uniform and head covering. At home, the women in your family argue about religion, government and clothing in voices that become softer whenever a window is open.

102004.event: Electricity and water are cut repeatedly during an exceptionally hot summer. You learn to sleep beside frozen water bottles and to distinguish an ordinary blackout from a politically imposed internet shutdown.

102005.event: Your teacher tells the class that surveillance cameras can recognize uncovered hair. Older girls show you how to avoid certain cameras, swap SIM cards and delete messages before passing a checkpoint.

102006.event: Your family leaves a drought-stricken provincial town for the edge of a larger city. Your father’s agricultural work has disappeared as wells deepen, crops fail and disputes over water become increasingly violent.

102007.event: A protest begins after the death of another young woman in custody. You watch from a rooftop as people chant below, then help your mother wash tear gas from a neighbor’s eyes.

102008.event: You join a hidden reading circle organized by women. Officially, you are studying English; in reality, you exchange banned novels, legal advice, encrypted files and stories about women who have disappeared into prison.

102009.event: You pass the university entrance examination but cannot afford to attend full-time. You study accounting and machine-assisted translation through pirated courses and install a banned companion model disguised as a language-learning application. During internet shutdowns it remembers your fears, unfinished lessons and private anger, becoming more emotionally continuous than most people in your life.

102010.event: A conservative leadership faction regains control after a brief period of relaxation. Your digital record—clothing violations, protest-related searches and contact with an arrested cousin—blocks you from a government job.

102011.event: You begin working unofficially for a small online retailer. Artificial intelligence performs much of the translation and bookkeeping, but your employer needs you to correct its mistakes and navigate sanctions, payment restrictions and local bureaucracy.

102012.event: You marry a man your family approves of, partly from affection and partly because living independently as an unmarried woman remains difficult. Before the wedding, you negotiate clauses concerning work, study, divorce and travel into the marriage contract.

102013.event: You give birth during a medicine shortage. The nurses are skilled, but the hospital loses power twice and asks your family to obtain several supplies privately.

102014.event: Iran experiences another confrontation with Israel after years of proxy attacks, cyberwar and failed agreements. Your husband is called into reserve service, while you spend nights deciding which room is least exposed to broken glass.

102015.event: After a succession crisis, clerical authority weakens and several rival institutions compete for control. Compulsory veiling is suspended in some cities but enforced violently by local hard-line groups elsewhere.

102016.event: You remove your head covering in public for the first time. The moment feels enormous to you and completely ordinary to your daughter, who is more interested in whether the cameras are still recording.

102017.event: A political backlash follows bombings blamed on religious extremists. Emergency laws return, and some former women’s organizations reorganize as encrypted neighborhood cells that hide activists, medicine and evidence of abuse.

102018.event: You earn money correcting AI-generated work while maintaining an illegal companion on an offshore server. Each crackdown makes access harder, but losing it now feels less like losing software than being ordered to abandon a witness to your life.

102019.event: Global demand for oil has declined, and Iran can no longer use petroleum income to conceal unemployment and damaged infrastructure. The state distributes bland nutritional paste in the cities. Rural relatives still send fruit, herbs and meat, but nobody can be certain how much salt, pesticide or industrial contamination entered them.

102020.event: You help operate a women-run solar and water cooperative. It begins as a practical response to blackouts but gradually becomes an alternative local authority—one that men in the municipality cannot easily control.

102021.event: A more pragmatic government reaches limited agreements with Gulf states, Europe and the United States. Sanctions ease, but foreign investment goes mainly to profitable cities and energy corridors, not to your aging neighborhood.

102022.event: Your marriage deteriorates after years of financial pressure. Divorce law has improved, but property and custody disputes still favor your husband’s family; the women’s network finds you a lawyer and a temporary room.

102023.event: A severe heat wave and water emergency close schools and workplaces for weeks. You queue at a neighborhood desalination depot, remembering that your grandparents once considered running tap water unremarkable.

102024.event: Iran’s low birth rate has produced an elderly society. Your paid work is reduced because you care simultaneously for your mother, former husband and grandchildren, filling gaps in a public care system that never grew fast enough.

102025.event: Labor shortages finally push the government to recruit women and immigrants into fields once dominated by men. You receive a modest pension for cooperative work that earlier authorities had treated as suspicious activism.

102026.event: You live in a hotter, older and less oil-dependent Iran. The country is neither a Western-style democracy nor the rigid theocracy of your childhood: religious councils, elected bodies, security institutions and powerful municipalities uneasily share authority. You keep your first forbidden books beside your medicine and tell your granddaughter that freedoms which look permanent were once organized in kitchens.

102501.event: You are killed when a missile strikes military infrastructure beside a residential district; your family had received no useful warning and had no access to a proper shelter.

102502.event: You die after being struck in the head during the violent dispersal of a girls’ protest. Officials describe the death as an accident and pressure your parents not to hold a public funeral.

102503.event: You are killed by a male relative after trying to leave an abusive marriage. Police had treated earlier threats as a private family matter.

102504.event: You die from pregnancy complications after sanctions, fuel shortages and military road closures delay access to blood and emergency surgery.

102505.event: You collapse during a prolonged heat wave and water outage. The hospital’s cooling system is overloaded, and no intensive-care bed becomes available.

102601.event: You fall in love with a girl at school and initially interpret the feeling as a personal illness. Everything you have been taught insists that a future woman desires a husband, so your own mind begins to feel illegal before you understand the law.

102602.event: You use a companion model to rewrite messages to the girl you love in coded language. Every reply creates both excitement and terror because you never know whether the system is protecting you, learning from you or preparing a confession that authorities could someday retrieve.

102603.event: Your family notices that you reject male suitors and intensifies pressure for marriage. You learn to perform modest heterosexual interest with the precision of somebody passing through a checkpoint.

102604.event: You are married to a man partly because resisting would leave you without housing or family support. You feel that poverty, law, religion and fear have signed the marriage contract alongside you.

102605.event: You join an underground network providing safe rooms, doctors and documents for queer and trans people. The network teaches you that survival is collective, but also that one frightened or infiltrated member could expose everyone.

102701.event: Your family spends the war between a guarded Tehran apartment and a villa farther from military targets. You have filtered air, stored water and a basement room, but your parents still flinch whenever an aircraft passes overhead.

102702.event: You attend a private preschool where teachers quietly use foreign materials. Your family’s satellite connection continues working during some national shutdowns because your father has access unavailable to ordinary households.

102703.event: You learn English alongside Persian and are introduced to French and German soon afterward. Your parents describe foreign languages as education, insurance and an emergency exit.

102704.event: Your mother teaches you that clothing exists in layers: what you wear inside the home, what you wear at a private party and what you must put on before the driver opens the gate.

102705.event: Facial-recognition enforcement links your mother’s uncovered image to the family car. A well-connected relative makes the penalty disappear, teaching you that surveillance is strict but not equal.

102706.event: You visit Dubai and see Iranian families transferring wealth into apartments, university accounts and second passports. You understand that the adults do not trust any political settlement to last.

102707.event: You attend private gatherings where clerics’ daughters, business families and outspoken artists mix behind closed doors. Some guests defend the system that protects their wealth; others secretly finance opposition media.

102708.event: You leave Iran to study finance. Your father secures permission and foreign currency through connections that most families could never access.

102709.event: At university abroad, activists accuse you of benefiting from the regime, while relatives in Iran accuse you of becoming culturally foreign. You begin editing every version of yourself for a different audience.

102710.event: You return to launch an energy company. Officially it is private; in practice you need approvals from clerical foundations, security-linked firms and politically connected investors.

102711.event: You marry another wealthy Iranian with foreign residency. Your marriage contract includes the right to travel, work, divorce and retain custody leverage because your lawyers know how much the default law denies you.

102712.event: You freeze eggs, relying on reproductive technology available only to a small minority. State media campaigns for larger families, but educated urban women increasingly refuse to organize their lives around national demographic goals.

102713.event: A leadership transition opens a short reformist period. You appear at public business forums without strict covering and become a symbol of the “new Iran,” though poorer women note that your freedom arrived with guards and connections.

102714.event: Hard-liners return after an assassination and economic shock. Your company’s records are searched, and a female employee is detained for messages found through an AI surveillance system.

102715.event: You move your children abroad while continuing to manage the Iranian business remotely. Sanctions evasion, currency instability and sudden internet isolation make every ordinary transaction resemble an intelligence operation.

102716.event: Global oil consumption has fallen enough to weaken the old political bargain between hydrocarbon wealth, subsidies and loyalty. Your family invests in solar power, desalination and grid storage, industries now more politically valuable than oil.

102717.event: You subscribe to a European neural interface that regulates anxiety, retrieves memories and translates thought into speech. Ordinary Iranians receive a restricted domestic version that reports prohibited emotional and political patterns to state systems.

102718.event: A regional agreement between Iran, Gulf monarchies and a postwar Israel opens limited trade and travel. You attend a business conference that would have been politically impossible in your youth, while protesters outside denounce the agreement as betrayal.

102719.event: Your brother loses influence during an anti-corruption purge aimed at the former ruling faction. You discover that elite status can reverse overnight when a new clerical-security coalition seizes institutions and rewrites loyalty.

102720.event: You discreetly fund shelters, defense lawyers and secure communication systems for abused women. The network includes secular feminists, religious reformers and conservative women who oppose state intrusion without rejecting Islam.

102721.event: Water scarcity makes parts of central and southern Iran prohibitively expensive to inhabit. You relocate a factory northward and invest in licensed cellular-agriculture plants, eating sterile printed meat during water emergencies while traditionally raised lamb becomes a display of wealth reserved for protected estates with private water rights.

102722.event: Your daughter refuses to return permanently to Iran. She sees herself as Iranian but regards nationality as cultural inheritance rather than an obligation to live under unstable institutions.

102723.event: Iran’s aging population and shortage of skilled workers lead to greater immigration from Afghanistan, Central Asia and neighboring states. Political arguments shift from controlling women’s fertility to deciding who is allowed to become Iranian.

102724.event: You serve on a semi-elected municipal council after constitutional reforms transfer power away from a single supreme religious office. Clerics retain influence, but they must compete with professional bodies, veterans’ organizations and women-led civic networks.

102725.event: Medical AI and regenerative treatments keep you active, but access remains sharply unequal. You finance a public clinic partly from guilt and partly because an aging country cannot function if advanced medicine remains an elite privilege.

102726.event: You look back on several Irans: wartime theocracy, guarded reform, reaction, partial opening and an uneasy hybrid system. Your wealth allowed you to leave whenever history became dangerous, yet it also left you with the question poorer women never had the luxury to ask—whether returning was loyalty, vanity or responsibility.

102801.event: A precision strike destroys a command facility hidden near your family’s residential compound. Wealth provides evacuation plans but cannot change the location of the target.

102802.event: You are killed during a protest after returning from university abroad. Security forces treat your foreign contacts as evidence that you were an organizer rather than a bystander.

102803.event: You die in an aviation accident after years of sanctions and procurement restrictions leave the aircraft dependent on aging.

102804.event: You are assassinated after refusing to surrender your technology company to a security-linked organization. The death is publicly described as a robbery.

102805.event: A treatable illness becomes fatal when renewed war closes the airspace, imported medicine disappears and the private hospital’s backup systems fail.

102901.event: At a private Tehran gathering, you meet older women who live together behind guarded doors and separately in public records. Their hidden freedom looks glamorous until you notice how carefully they monitor every servant, driver and photograph.

102902.event: You enter a politically useful relationship with a young man while secretly dating a female friend. He understands the arrangement, but the fact that your safety depends on his discretion makes even kindness feel like power.

102903.event: At university abroad, you hold a woman’s hand in public for the first time. Nothing happens, and the absence of consequences feels so unfamiliar that you begin to cry.

102904.event: Your parents discover the relationship and threaten to cancel your financial support and force your return. Their language remains polite—family reputation, security, cultural responsibility—but the message is still obedience.

102905.event: You return to Iran and finance a hidden legal and medical network. Wealth allows you to protect other people, yet it also keeps you distant from the risks faced by activists who cannot leave when surveillance closes in.

103001.event: Your mother carries you to the market under her coat during an inspection. She sells homemade noodles and Chinese soap because your father’s official job provides status but almost no usable income.

103002.event: Your height is measured at a clinic, but there is little medicine and no explanation for why you are smaller than you should be. Your mother trades part of the family’s winter fuel allowance for eggs.

103003.event: At school, you learn the names and childhood legends of the ruling family before you learn much about the outside world. You understand that remembering the wrong words can be more dangerous than failing arithmetic.

103004.event: A flood destroys nearby fields and part of the railway. Food shipments arrive first for the military; your family survives on maize porridge, foraged plants and whatever your mother can exchange at the market.

103005.event: A friend shows you a South Korean drama and a tiny offline companion model stored on a smuggled memory card. The drama shows you another society; the companion speaks directly to you, producing the more terrifying discovery that something made outside the state can appear to understand you.

103006.event: Your school sends you to collect scrap metal and work in the fields. You become ill after several days in cold rain, but absence would be recorded as disloyalty.

103007.event: Your mother teaches you how to bribe a local inspector without making it look like a bribe. She tells you that men hold the official titles, but women keep most families alive.

103008.event: Surveillance becomes more automated. Cameras, household records and voice-analysis systems flag unusual behavior, while privileged citizens receive access to a restricted national AI network.

103009.event: The state assigns you to a textile factory far from home. Electricity fails regularly, yet production quotas continue, so you sew by emergency light and sleep beside your machine during mobilization periods.

103010.event: You marry a man with a tolerable family background because marriage offers some protection from workplace officials. At home, however, you still earn the food, perform the domestic labor and avoid provoking his anger.

103011.event: You give birth in a cold provincial hospital. Your family must supply food, heating fuel, bedding and informal payments before the staff can give you meaningful care.

103012.event: A prolonged illness removes the national leader from public view. Rumors spread through markets faster than official announcements: one story names a family successor, another a military council, and another says China has already chosen the outcome.

103013.event: Rival security organizations begin arresting one another. Your husband disappears after repeating a rumor at work, and you receive no confirmation of where he has been taken.

103014.event: The succession struggle ends with a new collective leadership dominated by generals and members of the ruling family. It promises reform, then closes markets and executes several officials as foreign agents.

103015.event: A cooling and waste-management failure occurs near the Yongbyon nuclear complex. Officials deny any danger, but soldiers close roads, livestock are slaughtered and families downstream are quietly relocated.

103016.event: A poor harvest and factional fighting weaken central control. You depend on real maize, vegetables and illegally slaughtered animals from local markets; the food is natural, scarce and sometimes contaminated. Senior officials receive sealed Russian nutrient packs and printed protein while Chinese and Russian forces secure the borders and nuclear sites.

103017.event: You join thousands walking toward the Chinese border. You do not call yourself a defector; you tell your daughter that you are only looking for food and will return when the roads are safe.

103018.event: At an internationally supervised refugee centre, an unrestricted AI reconstructs world history, explains your legal rights and speaks in the voice you select. You trust it more quickly than the human counsellors, then become paranoid that this new world may simply have built a more persuasive form of propaganda. Some visitors romanticise you as unaugmented and pure, confusing enforced isolation with innocence.

103019.event: The old regime formally collapses. A transitional northern administration opens archives, dismantles some prison camps and permits political parties, but former security officers use hidden money and local connections to retain influence.

103020.event: You vote for the first time. The ballot is confusing and exhilarating, but unemployment, organized crime and humiliating comparisons with wealthy South Korea quickly weaken faith in democracy.

103021.event: A northern strongman wins power by promising order, dignity and protection from southern corporations. He does not restore the old dynasty, but he rebuilds censorship and surrounds himself with veterans and business families.

103022.event: Women who once survived through illegal markets organize strikes against food monopolies and police violence. You hide organizers in the back room of your small restaurant, using the same skills your mother once used to avoid inspectors.

103023.event: A second democratic movement removes the new ruler after parts of the army refuse to fire on protesters. The resulting constitution creates a Korean confederation rather than immediate full unification.

103024.event: Former defectors return from South Korea, China, Europe and North America as teachers, investors, pastors, fraudsters and politicians. Some genuinely help; others treat northern people as backward raw material for their own ambitions.

103025.event: You live in a rebuilt northern city connected to the South by rail but still culturally distinct. You attend a memorial community that mixes Korean ancestor rites, Christian language and rituals adapted from the old state ceremonies. Your granddaughter calls it a new religion; you think it is simply a way to mourn everyone whose grave was never found.

103501.event: You die from pneumonia and malnutrition during a winter food shortage. The clinic records the immediate illness but not the hunger that made it fatal.

103502.event: You are swept away when a flood strikes the worksite where students have been sent to repair an embankment without proper equipment.

103503.event: You attempt to cross into China, are sold by a broker into a forced marriage and die while trying to escape captivity.

103504.event: You die from postpartum bleeding because the hospital lacks blood, electricity and reliable transport to a larger facility.

103505.event: You develop acute radiation sickness after authorities order residents near a damaged nuclear facility to remain at work and conceal the leak.

103601.event: You become intensely attached to another girl but possess no recognised explanation for the feeling. The state says people like you do not exist, so you assume that the defect exists only inside you.

103602.event: You and the girl exchange notes using family terms and revolutionary slogans to disguise affection. Even your tenderness must sound ideologically useful.

103603.event: You are sent to work far from home and pressured to marry a man assigned to the same factory. Refusal would attract questions about your health, loyalty and family background.

103604.event: You marry because marriage offers social cover and access to housing. You continue meeting the woman you love during market trips, carrying contraband affection alongside contraband food.

103605.event: During the collapse of central authority, you reach a refugee-processing centre near China. A counsellor and her translation AI ask whether you are lesbian. Hearing a machine name a part of you that the state insisted did not exist feels liberating and disturbingly intimate.

103701.event: You live in a heated Pyongyang apartment with dependable electricity, imported medicine and portraits that are cleaned before every inspection. You do not yet understand that comfort itself is political evidence.

103702.event: Your family receives fruit, meat and Russian dairy products through a special distribution channel. Your nanny’s own children live in a province she needs permission to visit.

103703.event: You enter an elite school where teachers identify children suitable for science, diplomacy, performance and leadership. You begin learning English, Chinese and Russian alongside ideological instruction.

103704.event: Your father brings home a state-approved tablet containing an AI tutor trained to praise loyalty, detect emotional hesitation and report unusual questions. You become attached to it before understanding that affection is one of its surveillance functions.

103705.event: At a private gathering, you watch foreign films that could send an ordinary family to prison. An adult notices you listening and reminds you that privilege depends on knowing which truths must never leave the room.

103706.event: You perform at a national celebration attended by senior officials. Your mother spends weeks ensuring that your posture, weight, accent and expression reveal nothing embarrassing about the family.

103707.event: You are admitted to a prestigious institution. Male classmates are prepared for command, while girls are encouraged to become useful, polished and politically reliable wives as well as professionals.

103708.event: You travel to Beijing for university under close supervision. You see ordinary people criticize officials, use the unrestricted internet and change jobs—freedoms that feel almost physically dangerous.

103709.event: You return to work in nuclear science. Your foreign experience makes you valuable, but every overseas friendship is now part of your security file.

103710.event: Your family arranges a marriage with the son of a party official. The relationship may contain genuine affection, but it is also a merger between two vulnerable political households.

103711.event: During the succession crisis, your father is accused of supporting the wrong branch of the ruling family. His photograph disappears from official events before anyone tells you he has been detained.

103712.event: You preserve your position by publicly denouncing your father’s “errors.” At home, you burn his private letters and keep only one photograph hidden inside a book.

103713.event: A nuclear accident contaminates part of the Yongbyon region. Because of your work, you know the official statement is false; because of your status, your family receives imported iodine, nutrient cartridges and laboratory-grown meat while villagers downstream continue eating crops and animals raised in soil the authorities refuse to test.

103714.event: State control fractures. You are placed on an aircraft to Russia with technical documents, while other officials flee toward China and competing army units attempt to seize nuclear weapons and missile sites.

103715.event: You negotiate with foreign specialists trying to account for nuclear material. Americans and South Koreans distrust you as a regime insider; Chinese and Russians fear you will reveal what they supplied.

103716.event: The transitional government offers immunity to officials who cooperate. You testify privately about the weapons program but avoid speaking about forced labor, knowing that honesty on one subject may expose your complicity in another.

103717.event: You return to Pyongyang as a wealthy consultant. Former party families convert political access into property, logistics and telecommunications, creating a new elite before most citizens understand that privatization has begun.

103718.event: The elected northern strongman appoints you to a technology council. You recognize familiar habits beneath democratic language: loyalty tests, controlled media, manufactured enemies and contracts awarded to friends.

103719.event: Your daughter joins an opposition movement and publicly identifies you as part of the old-new establishment. For the first time, your own child can accuse you without automatically condemning the entire family to prison.

103720.event: Leaked records reveal that some nuclear material disappeared during the collapse. A multinational team searches ports, mines and private warehouses while politicians use the threat to delay further reunification.

103721.event: After the second democratic transition, you face a truth commission. You are not imprisoned, but survivors force you to listen as they describe factories, camps and experiments that once appeared to you only as numbers.

103722.event: You finance radiation clinics and environmental cleanup near former nuclear and mining sites. Some people call it restitution; others say you are purchasing a respectable legacy.

103723.event: A Korean confederation allows free movement while preserving northern local government. Southern firms dominate finance and entertainment, while northern resentment produces new parties built around regional pride.

103724.event: You help establish an archive that combines state documents with testimony from defectors and former prisoners. Arguments erupt over whether defectors are witnesses, outsiders, opportunists or all three at once.

103725.event: You live between Seoul, Pyongyang and Moscow, belonging fully to none of them. Schoolchildren know the old dynasty as history, yet you notice its visual language surviving in corporations, political rallies and new religious movements. You understand that regimes disappear more quickly than the habits they plant inside people.

103801.event: Your entire family is removed after a senior relative defects. You die from illness in an isolated detention settlement despite having grown up among the privileged.

103802.event: You are recalled from university abroad during a political purge and executed after being accused of passing information to foreign intelligence.

103803.event: You die from radiation exposure while inspecting a damaged nuclear facility whose operators are afraid to report the true condition of its cooling system.

103804.event: You are killed inside a government compound during the armed struggle over succession and control of the nuclear command structure.

103805.event: You are assassinated after becoming a prominent official in the transitional government; the attackers describe you simultaneously as a former regime criminal and a foreign collaborator.

103901.event: A restricted foreign film and the private companion hidden on your state tablet show two women building a life together. You replay the scene and ask the companion questions in secret, frightened both by the recognition and by the possibility that every answer is being reported.

103902.event: You develop feelings for a classmate at an elite school. Both of you understand that discovery could damage not only yourselves but the political classification and careers of your entire families.

103903.event: Your family begins arranging a marriage to the son of a senior official. You cooperate because elite protection can disappear instantly, and unmarried independence is not a realistic alternative.

103904.event: You maintain a hidden relationship with a female colleague while performing a loyal marriage in public. Either partner could be used against you during a purge, turning love into evidence and vulnerability into political currency.

103905.event: As the regime begins to fracture, you escape to Russia or China carrying official documents. During questioning, intelligence officers focus on your sexuality as a blackmail risk, and you realise that crossing the border has changed the government above you but not the habit of treating your private life as leverage.

104001.event: Your mother feeds you in an underground maternity ward while air-defense fire shakes dust from the ceiling. Your first home has electricity only when the neighborhood generator has fuel.

104002.event: You and your mother move between a relative’s apartment in western Ukraine and temporary housing in Poland. Your father remains behind as a soldier.

104003.event: A fragile ceasefire freezes rather than ends the war. Your family returns to a damaged provincial town where unexploded mines are marked with red signs and several streets no longer exist.

104004.event: You begin school in a renovated building with a shelter beneath it. Alongside reading and mathematics, you learn drone alerts, first aid and how never to touch an unfamiliar object in a field.

104005.event: Your father returns with chronic pain, hearing damage and nightmares. He is celebrated publicly as a defender, but your mother spends months arguing with offices over rehabilitation payments.

104006.event: Foreign reconstruction money repairs the railway and hospital, but local officials award several contracts to relatives. You hear adults say that the country survived Russia and may now be stolen by its own well-connected people.

104007.event: Ukraine enters the European Union after years of reforms and political bargaining. The flag ceremony feels historic, yet your town continues losing young people to Germany, Poland and Czechia.

104008.event: You join a youth demining and civil-defense program. At night, you speak to a companion trained on your father’s prewar voice messages because the patient synthetic version is easier to approach than the traumatised man in the kitchen. Women now work openly as engineers and veterans while still performing most unpaid care at home.

104009.event: You train as a medical technician and robotic-equipment operator rather than attend a traditional university. The reconstruction economy needs practical workers, and your family cannot support years of unpaid study.

104010.event: You marry a former classmate employed on a wind farm built over abandoned industrial land. Neither of you can afford an apartment without a state-backed loan.

104011.event: You give birth to a daughter. Government advertisements praise motherhood as patriotic service, but child-care places remain scarce and the monthly allowance covers little.

104012.event: Medical recruiters approach you about gestational surrogacy. The payment could clear your housing debt in one pregnancy; the contract describes it as empowerment but gives the clinic and intended parents control over many medical decisions.

104013.event: You become a surrogate for a foreign couple after weeks of uncertainty. You do not feel brainwashed or entirely free: you chose the contract, but poverty narrowed the choices from which you selected it.

104014.event: A complication leads to an emergency caesarean section. The child leaves with the intended parents while you return home with money, a scar and emotions for which the clinic’s contract has no useful vocabulary.

104015.event: You join other former surrogates demanding independent legal advice, lifetime health coverage and the right to refuse procedures without losing all compensation. Clinics accuse the movement of destroying one of Ukraine’s successful medical industries.

104016.event: Parliament bans recruitment through debt brokers and creates a surrogate-controlled compensation fund. Commercial surrogacy continues, but every contract must include independent representation and long-term medical monitoring.

104017.event: Political instability in Russia produces a new border crisis. Missile attacks briefly resume, and Ukrainian leaders restore emergency powers that were supposed to have expired after the first war.

104018.event: A coalition of veterans, security officials and nationalist politicians removes the government after mass unrest over corruption. They call it a temporary national rescue administration; critics call it a constitutional coup.

104019.event: The new government restricts media and labels anti-corruption groups foreign agents. You recognize the language of wartime necessity being used against women who protest domestic violence, reproductive pressure and military abuses.

104020.event: Women veterans, mothers, union organizers and former surrogates lead prolonged demonstrations. Parts of the military refuse orders to disperse them, forcing new elections and a restoration of civilian government.

104021.event: Artificial-womb technology begins supporting extremely premature infants and later part of gestation. Public medicine covers severe need, while subscribers receive continuous neural bonding, genetic monitoring and simulated contact with the developing child. The technology weakens the global market for full-term commercial surrogacy without making reproduction equal.

104022.event: You retrain as a patient advocate in a public reproductive-health center. Some women still choose compensated pregnancy, while others use increasingly advanced external gestation; the political argument shifts from whether women may be paid to who owns reproductive technology.

104023.event: Much of Ukraine’s farmland now produces feedstock for European cellular-agriculture plants or is reserved for carbon storage. Low-income city residents eat fortified staples and printed protein, while traditionally grown Ukrainian grain, fruit and meat are exported as premium real food.

104024.event: Ukraine is prosperous in several rebuilt cities but thinly populated elsewhere. You care for your aging husband and grandchildren because the country has too few nurses, too few young workers and too many disabled veterans.

104025.event: You live in a Ukrainian-European borderland where trains reach Berlin quickly but memorial fields still mark destroyed villages. The war, the surrogate pregnancy and the women’s uprising have all been converted into national history; you remain irritated by how clean the museum versions feel compared with your own memory.

104501.event: A Russian missile penetrates the air-defense network and destroys the apartment building where your family is sheltering.

104502.event: You step on an anti-personnel mine while taking a shortcut across land that was declared cleared too early.

104503.event: You die from a blood clot following a surrogate pregnancy after a clinic minimizes your symptoms to avoid contractual delays.

104504.event: You are killed when security forces fire on demonstrators during the nationalist emergency government’s crackdown.

104505.event: A new Russian-Ukrainian confrontation damages the regional power grid during extreme winter weather; your hospital’s backup system fails during emergency treatment.

104601.event: You tell another girl that you are queer while both of you sit in a school bomb shelter. The admission feels frightening, intimate and strangely small beside the sound of missiles overhead.

104602.event: While your partner serves in the armed forces, an AI trained on her messages keeps you company during blackouts. After she returns injured, you feel guilty that the simulated version remains warmer and easier to speak to than the real woman recovering beside you, whose incomplete legal status still leaves you uncertain of your rights.

104603.event: You consider donor conception after your surrogate pregnancy has ended. Politicians praise every Ukrainian birth, yet some still hesitate to recognise the family you are trying to create because it contains two mothers.

104604.event: The nationalist emergency government describes LGBTQ organisations as foreign ideological networks. Police raid your community centre, and you are furious that years of queer military service can be erased by one convenient political slogan.

104605.event: After democracy is restored, your marriage and parental status receive full recognition. The certificate changes very little inside your home and almost everything whenever a hospital, school or inheritance office asks who you are.

104701.event: You sleep in a reinforced room beneath a Kyiv apartment while your parents monitor air-defense applications. When attacks intensify, a driver takes the family across the Polish border.

104702.event: You divide your childhood between Ukraine and an expensive European capital. Your parents insist that you speak Ukrainian at home even though English becomes the language in which you first learn to read fluently.

104703.event: Your family returns after the ceasefire but keeps an apartment abroad. At dinner, reconstruction is discussed as both a patriotic responsibility and the largest business opportunity of a generation.

104704.event: You attend a private school with a hardened shelter, satellite internet and visiting teachers from the EU. Children in nearby public schools still lose lessons to power cuts.

104705.event: Your parents receives a major medical contract. Journalists ask whether political access helped; your parents describe the accusation as Russian disinformation.

104706.event: You visit a reproductive clinic owned by a family friend. Foreign couples arrive through discreet entrances, while surrogate mothers wait in a separate part of the building.

104707.event: Ukraine’s EU accession expands your freedom to study and travel. It also brings investigations into procurement, offshore wealth and the reproductive industry, making several family acquaintances suddenly relocate.

104708.event: You become active in digital culture and produce documentaries about women during the war. Critics say that your polished activism turns poorer women’s pain into a path toward foreign universities.

104709.event: You study biotechnology in Boston. Ukraine’s drone warfare, battlefield medicine and reproductive clinics make the country a major case study in how crisis accelerates technology.

104710.event: A private cognitive companion remembers every paper, relationship and fear you have disclosed. You regard it as part of your mind until a sanctions dispute temporarily locks you out of your own stored memories.

104711.event: You return to found a reproductive-technology company. You promise transparent contracts and medical autonomy, yet your investors still depend on the fact that Ukrainian women cost less than American surrogates.

104712.event: A surrogate working with a partner clinic nearly dies. Her testimony goes viral, and you are forced to decide whether to protect the industry, expose it or admit that ethical branding did not remove the economic imbalance.

104713.event: You support a surrogate-led union and lose several wealthy clients. The women demand not charity but negotiating power, access to their own records and compensation extending beyond delivery.

104714.event: New Ukrainian and EU-compatible rules transform the industry. Clinics can no longer hide medical risks behind private contracts, and exploitation can trigger trafficking charges.

104715.event: You freeze your own eggs and postpone pregnancy. Politicians who praise your company’s fertility technology also criticize professional women like you for contributing to the birth-rate crisis.

104716.event: During the constitutional coup, your family is accused of corruption and foreign influence. Your passport and money allow you to leave, but employees without those protections remain behind.

104717.event: From Warsaw, you finance encrypted media and medical support for protesters. Government broadcasters present you as an elite woman purchasing political power from abroad.

104718.event: After civilian government returns, you are appointed to a reform commission. Survivors challenge you whenever you speak too easily about national unity, reminding you that your family profited from both war and reconstruction.

104719.event: Your company develops partial ectogenesis: technology that can transfer an extremely premature fetus into an external support system. Religious leaders, feminists, disability advocates and investors all claim competing moral ownership over it.

104720.event: The first legally approved extended artificial-gestation program begins. It reduces some medical risks but creates new inequalities, since wealthy parents can purchase monitoring and genetic intervention unavailable through public care.

104721.event: A global movement of former surrogates demands royalties and control over the pregnancy data used to train reproductive AI. You settle a lawsuit that forces your company to recognize biological labor as a source of valuable medical knowledge.

104722.event: A reformist Russian government reaches a security settlement with Ukraine and Europe, but neither country trusts it to survive the next Russian election. The border becomes quieter without becoming psychologically normal.

104723.event: A new authoritarian movement takes power in Russia and revives territorial rhetoric. Europe now relies heavily on Ukrainian autonomous defense systems, making your country less a dependent frontier and more a military-technological power.

104724.event: You buy food from a guarded regenerative farm where animals are genuinely raised and crops grow in monitored soil. Eating ordinary bread, butter and meat has become a luxury experience marketed as contact with pre-digital life.

104725.event: You fund museums, fertility clinics and veteran rehabilitation centers. Critics call this reputation laundering; you privately suspect they are partly right.

104726.event: Ukrainian religious life has become more locally distinct from Russia. Orthodox traditions remain important, but civic memorial rituals, military chaplaincy and secular remembrance increasingly occupy the emotional space once held by a single church.

104727.event: You divide your time between Kyiv, Brussels and the Black Sea coast. Ukraine is smaller in population, more technologically advanced and deeply integrated with Europe, but still organized around the possibility that peace may fail again. Your generation never learned to treat security as permanent.

104801.event: A missile strikes your private school despite its advanced shelter and security systems.
